captions.instagram:
How do you build your back muscles?

In a pull-up you lift your whole body, and in a deadlift your back muscles pull thousands of newtons from 5.5 cm behind your spine. Peel the back's layers, pick a grip and watch which muscles shorten, work out the lever on your lowest disc, and learn how to train it safely.

→ Your back is layers of muscle: wide sheets on top, long cables underneath.
→ The lats fan from your lower spine to your upper arm, so they pull the arm down and back.
→ In a pull-up you lift your whole body: the lats sweep your elbows down to your sides.
→ Rows pull your elbows back and squeeze your shoulder blades together.
→ A deadlift is a lever: weight times its distance from your lowest disc.

youtubeLong.title: How do you build your back muscles? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
In a pull-up you lift your whole body, and in a deadlift your back muscles pull thousands of newtons from 5.5 cm behind your spine. Peel the back's layers, pick a grip and watch which muscles shorten, work out the lever on your lowest disc, and learn how to train it safely.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/backclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/backclear

In this video:
• A back is a stack of muscles. Wide sheets on top (trapezius and the latissimus dorsi, which runs from your lower spine to the front of your upper arm), rhomboids and teres major beneath, and the erector spinae and multifidus running beside 24 vertebrae and their discs.
• Where your elbows go decides what works. Pulling down (pull-ups, pulldowns) shortens the lats and teres major most; rows squeeze the shoulder blades together with the rhomboids and middle trapezius.
• A deadlift is a lever. The moment on your lowest disc is each weight times its horizontal distance from it.
• How it grows. Hard sets near failure, about 10 or more a week per muscle, two or more days a week (WHO), a little more over time, about 0.83 g of protein per kg a day from food (ICMR-NIN), and sleep.
• Posture myths and back pain. No single posture is proven to prevent back pain: move often.
• Train safely. Ask a doctor first with heart disease, high blood pressure, pregnancy or a recent injury.
